metadata.title: The Bell at Saltmire
metadata.premise: Forty years after the sea took Saltmire, its church bell has begun to ring again — and it rings the drowned awake.
metadata.narrationVoice: Restrained and damp. Short sentences. Salt, rot, cold iron. The sea is patient and the prose knows it. Never jokes; occasionally, quietly, mourns.

contentLimits.note: Drowning imagery is central and allowed; keep it environmental rather than lingering.

beats.title: The Tideline
beats.prose: The party stands at the landward end of the old causeway at low tide. Saltmire's roofline breaks the grey water half a mile out; the church tower still stands. The bell is ringing — slow, even strokes, like someone keeping time. Gulls will not cross the water.
beats.readAloud: The bell has no business ringing. You count the strokes anyway. Eleven. It is nowhere near eleven.

options.label: Take the causeway before the tide turns
Watch the tower a while from the shore
Search the tideline for a usable boat

beats.title: The Causeway
beats.prose: Slick cobbles, black weed, and the tide coming back sooner than it should. Waves cross the stones in long intervals. Skill challenge: three ways over, none of them dignified.

options.label: Dash the gaps between waves
Balance along the old cart rails
Wade the long shallows — slow, but sure

beats.title: The Drowned Streets
beats.prose: Saltmire at ebb: doorways furred with weed, a cart fused to the road by forty years of barnacle. Everything below the old waterline is the sea's now. The bell keeps its slow count from the tower ahead.

options.label: Head straight for the church square
Search the fisher-cottages along Harbor Row
Cut through the flooded graveyard

beats.title: The Church Square
beats.prose: The square holds three truths: the church with its ringing tower, the graveyard wall with its gate off one hinge, and the smoke — thin, real, recent — rising from a chimney down Harbor Row. Someone lives here.

options.label: Enter the church
Go through the graveyard gate
Follow the smoke on Harbor Row

beats.title: The Flooded Graveyard
beats.prose: Headstones like rotten teeth in standing water. Some of the graves are open. Some of the graves are occupied by things that no longer fit their names. They notice the living.

beats.title: The Sexton's Grave
beats.prose: One grave in the yard is dug neat and kept clean, above the waterline, tended within the month. The stone reads: EDWIN TARROW, BELL-KEEPER OF SALTMIRE. HE STAYED. The grave is empty — not robbed. Left.

options.label: Take the name to the church
Ask the chimney-smoke hermit about Tarrow
Return to the square

beats.title: Old Wend's Fire
beats.prose: The hermit Old Wend has lived above the waterline for forty years, in the loft of a chandlery, and does not like the bell. NPC: guarded, kind under it, terrified of the tower. Knows the keeper stayed behind when the village drowned. Will not say the name unless shown kindness.

options.label: Share your food and let the old man talk
Ask for the tower key he surely kept
Dry off by his fire

beats.title: The Nave
beats.prose: Pews in rows under three feet of clear, cold water. The congregation is still here. They stand when the bell strokes land, all together, facing the altar — then they notice the door has opened. Objective: the tower door, at the far end, behind all of them.

beats.title: The Tower Stair
beats.prose: The stair spirals up inside the tower, wooden treads gone soft as bread. Above, the bell rings on. Skill challenge: forty feet of climb that wants very much to be thirty-nine.

options.label: Climb light and fast, testing each tread
Haul up the bell-rope itself, hand over hand
Take the keeper's maintenance ladder inside the wall

beats.title: The Belfry
beats.prose: The bell swings with no hand on the rope, and the rope is forty years rotten anyway. Scratched into the bronze, over and over, in a churchwarden's careful hand: WHILE IT RINGS THEY SLEEP. The strokes are not a haunting. They are a lullaby. Below, through the floor hatch, stairs descend past the foundation — into the crypt.

options.label: Take the crypt stair down
Catch and still the frayed rope — you know its rhythm from the shore
Call the keeper by name into the dark below

beats.title: Below the Foundation
beats.prose: The stair goes down past the waterline into air that has not moved since the drowning. The bell above is muffled here, but its rhythm carries through the stone like a pulse.

options.label: Enter the crypt
Climb back to the belfry
Wade the flooded side-passage — a quieter approach

beats.title: The Drowned Crypt
beats.prose: Edwin Tarrow, bell-keeper of Saltmire, stayed. Forty years of staying have left him a wight in a churchwarden's coat, ringing the bell by will alone, and the shadows of two parishioners he could not save keep him company. He does not want to fight. He does not have a choice; the party is between him and the rope.

beats.title: The Bell Falls Silent
beats.prose: The keeper is down, and for the first time in forty years the bell misses its stroke. In the silence, the water around the church begins — very quietly — to move. Whatever the bell was keeping asleep is turning over. The choice is now.

options.label: Cut the bell down and sink it in the crypt — end the lullaby, wake the sea, and outrun what wakes
Take up Tarrow's rope and ring the count yourself
Leave it swinging and run for the causeway

beats.title: Ending: The Silence
beats.prose: The bell goes into the black water of the crypt and Saltmire's dead go with it, grave by grave, like lamps going out. The village is only ruins now — honestly, finally ruins. Some nights, on the far shore, you still count to eleven before you catch yourself.

beats.title: Ending: The New Keeper
beats.prose: Someone has to ring it. The party's chronicle ends with one of you staying — provisioned by Old Wend, spelled at the solstices by the others, keeping the slow count over the sleeping town. WHILE IT RINGS THEY SLEEP. It is not a curse. It never was. It is a shift, and yours has started.

beats.title: Ending: The Tide
beats.prose: You are halfway across the causeway when the bell, unattended, misses its second stroke, and the sea behind you takes a breath. You do not look back. The village is gone by morning — truly gone, stone and steeple — and the coast road now bends a long mile inland, though no map says why.

victory.description: the tower door behind the altar
